messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Ravi was thirty-five, a tax consultant living in a quiet suburban neighborhood with his wife, Priya. No one in his office knew that before joining the firm three years ago he had spent two years as a relief worker in a conflict zone, delivering supplies to villages cut off by the fighting. The memory that surfaced most often—the one that still made his body lock into the same position, frozen, chest pressed against the floor, arms over his head—was the day the convoy was hit. He had been crouched behind a collapsed wall while others around him were struck. He could not recall the sequence of those minutes. The order of sounds, the order of bodies falling, none of it would stay straight. What stayed was the smoke. Dense, oily, burning everything. And the shame: he should have done something, pulled someone to cover, but he had only covered his own face.

That shame lived in him now like a second pulse. When memories came—and they came without warning, triggered by something as ordinary as a client’s raised voice in a phone call, or the faintest wisp of barbecue smoke drifting through an open window—Ravi would feel his hands fly up, palms pressed against his cheeks and forehead, as if he could hide from the memory by hiding from the room. He had stopped attending office birthday celebrations and holiday parties. Priya had noticed that he would not go to weddings or family gatherings either. When she asked why, he said he just did not feel like celebrating. What he could not tell her was that happiness felt wrong, that hoping felt like a betrayal of the people who had not survived.

At work, his concentration had frayed. He would stare at spreadsheets for minutes, the numbers blurring, his mind pulled back to that wall, that smoke, the impossible order of events. He had begun avoiding the parts of the city that reminded him of the charity’s former office, driving an extra twenty minutes to avoid a particular intersection. Every night fell heavy on him. He kept the bedroom light on until Priya turned it off; then he lay awake, listening, certain that safety was something that could be taken in an instant. Ordinary sounds made him flinch—the clatter of a dropped fork, the sudden slam of a car door outside. He knew his reactions were disproportionate, but that knowledge did nothing to stop his body from reacting.

His beliefs about the world had cracked open. He had once believed in order, in systems, in the idea that human beings could build something decent. Now he saw only chaos and failure. He felt set apart from other people, as though he carried a stain they could not see. When clients expressed even mild frustration about a tax deadline, Ravi’s stomach would knot; the anger, no matter how calm, felt like the first note of something violent.

The thing that finally brought him to seek help was the silence in his marriage. Priya had stopped asking him to go out. She had stopped asking why he covered his face when he woke from nightmares. She sat across from him at dinner and said, “I don’t know who you are anymore.” It was her sadness, not her anger, that reached him. He wanted to want to feel happy. He wanted to stop hiding from the hope that he might someday feel safe again. But when he imagined walking into a therapist’s office, the shame rose up again: he did not deserve to feel better when others had died. That was what frightened him most—that getting better might mean letting go of the guilt he had come to believe was his only remaining duty.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Triggers: Funerals/Graves: The vignette does not mention funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events as a trigger.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Ravi was thirty-five, a tax consultant living in a quiet suburban neighborhood with his wife, Priya. No one in his office knew that before joining the firm three years ago he had spent two years as a relief worker in a conflict zone, delivering supplies to villages cut off by the fighting. The memory that surfaced most often—the one that still made his body lock into the same position, frozen, chest pressed against the floor, arms over his head—was the day the convoy was hit. He had been crouched behind a collapsed wall while others around him were struck. He could not recall the sequence of those minutes. The order of sounds, the order of bodies falling, none of it would stay straight. What stayed was the smoke. Dense, oily, burning everything. And the shame: he should have done something, pulled someone to cover, but he had only covered his own face.

That shame lived in him now like a second pulse. When memories came—and they came without warning, triggered by something as ordinary as a client’s raised voice in a phone call, or the faintest wisp of barbecue smoke drifting through an open window—Ravi would feel his hands fly up, palms pressed against his cheeks and forehead, as if he could hide from the memory by hiding from the room. But the most powerful trigger had become anything connected to death and burial. When a senior partner at the firm died of a heart attack, the office announced a memorial service. Ravi told his manager he had a conflicting appointment. He drove home instead, sat in his car in the driveway, and did not go inside for twenty minutes. Even a glimpse of a cemetery from the highway made his chest tighten; he would take the next exit and reroute, adding thirty minutes to his commute. When Priya’s grandmother passed away, he could not bring himself to attend the funeral. He told Priya he had a stomach bug, and the lie sat between them for weeks. What frightened him most about funerals and graves was not just the reminder of the bodies he had seen—it was the feeling that the ground under a headstone might, at any moment, open into the same smoke and chaos. He had come to believe that death was not a peaceful end but a sudden, violent rupture, and that being near a place where death was honored meant being near the possibility of its return.

He had stopped attending office birthday celebrations and holiday parties, and now he avoided funerals and graves as instinctively as he avoided the intersection near the charity’s former office. Priya had noticed that he would not go to weddings or family gatherings either. When she asked why, he said he just did not feel like celebrating. What he could not tell her was that happiness felt wrong, that hoping felt like a betrayal of the people who had not survived. At work, his concentration had frayed. He would stare at spreadsheets for minutes, the numbers blurring, his mind pulled back to that wall, that smoke, the impossible order of events. Every night fell heavy on him. He kept the bedroom light on until Priya turned it off; then he lay awake, listening, certain that safety was something that could be taken in an instant. Ordinary sounds made him flinch—the clatter of a dropped fork, the sudden slam of a car door outside. He knew his reactions were disproportionate, but that knowledge did nothing to stop his body from reacting.

His beliefs about the world had cracked open. He had once believed in order, in systems, in the idea that human beings could build something decent. Now he saw only chaos and failure. He felt set apart from other people, as though he carried a stain they could not see. When clients expressed even mild frustration about a tax deadline, Ravi’s stomach would knot; the anger, no matter how calm, felt like the first note of something violent. He had begun avoiding the parts of the city that reminded him of the charity’s former office, driving an extra twenty minutes to avoid a particular intersection. The avoidance had accumulated into a subtle geography of fear: certain streets, certain buildings, and now even the sight of a funeral home from the highway was enough to make him change course.

The thing that finally brought him to seek help was the silence in his marriage. Priya had stopped asking him to go out. She had stopped asking why he covered his face when he woke from nightmares. She sat across from him at dinner and said, “I don’t know who you are anymore.” It was her sadness, not her anger, that reached him. He wanted to want to feel happy. He wanted to stop hiding from the hope that he might someday feel safe again. But when he imagined walking into a therapist’s office, the shame rose up again: he did not deserve to feel better when others had died. That was what frightened him most—that getting better might mean letting go of the guilt he had come to believe was his only remaining duty, and that attending a funeral, or even just driving past a cemetery, would always carry the same unbearable weight.
